rv.q: Jack Thorne's 'The Motive and the Cue,' is a rapier-witted and stirring love-letter to theatre, and to Hamlet, and to two of the play'
If you have any interest in the power of theatre, I urge you to catch a play that’s both an exploration of it and a remarkable vindication of it.
I liked this play when it opened earlier this year. Now I love it.
That ‘The Motive and The Cue’ has fast become almost as acclaimed seems so very fitting.
This is a play that thrives on the knowing exploitation of showbiz mythology.
It is the triumph of both play and performance that he is so much more than that.
The clash of these two theatrical greats, along with the glimpse behind the curtain of the creative process makes The Motive and the Cue a perfect production for any lover of theatre to experience.
The fraught tensions bubbling away as the emblem of the old guard slowly yields to the pin-up boy of the new feel real, urgent, and engrossing throughout.
One thing is for sure: it’s a play that epitomises the epithet ‘A love letter to theatre’.
Bolstered by immaculate work from its leads and a sharp, insightful script, it will likely be a late entry to many end of the year lists.

Sam Mendes and Jack Thorne have together created a brilliant piece of theatre, certainly one that’s fascinating to anyone with an interest in the industry, but equally entertaining for anyone who loves a good story.
Lifting the curtain on the rehearsal room and witnessing the process, rather than watching the end product, makes this an absolute must see for all theatre lovers.
Nevertheless, as a whole, this piece is hard to resist, especially after all the emotion of its rousing conclusion.
The resulting shape of The Motive and the Cue is both polished and full-blooded.

cn.t: Jack Thorne's rapier-witted drama about Gielgud directing Burton's 1964 Hamlet earns widespread acclaim as a stirring love letter to theatre, bolstered by stellar performances from Gatiss and Flynn in Sam Mendes' triumphant production.
